title: Ten healed, one returned (Luke 17:11–19)
hookLine: ten lepers healed; only a Samaritan comes back to say thank you

cards: Between Samaria and Galilee, at the edge of a village, ten men stand at a distance. They have to.

They have leprosy, the Bible's word for skin diseases that made a person unclean, and the law said they must live apart: no home, no work, no family's touch. At least one, we'll learn, is a Samaritan.
Trouble has put them all on the same road. They see Jesus coming, and they don't come closer. They lift up their voices.

teach.b: In the King James Bible they cry: "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us." He doesn't touch them or say be healed. He says: "Go shew yourselves unto the priests."
The law required a priest to confirm someone had recovered. But they haven't, yet. They have to start walking while still sick.

teach.h: AS THEY WENT, THEY WERE CLEANSED.
teach.b: "And it came to pass, that, as they went, they were cleansed."
Then the turn: "And one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, and with a loud voice glorified God, And fell down on his face at his feet, giving him thanks: and he was a Samaritan."
The same loud voice he'd used to beg, now used to praise.

Giving thanks, in Greek, is eucharisteo. Eu, good; charis, grace or gift. It's where the word Eucharist comes from, the name Catholics, Orthodox Christians, Anglicans and others use for communion, the great thanksgiving.
Jesus asks: "Were there not ten cleansed? but where are the nine?" To be fair, the nine were doing what they were told, heading to the priests. Luke never calls them ungrateful.
But only one turned around and came back first. Jesus calls him "this stranger," a foreigner. The outsider is the one who sees the gift.

teach.h: THY FAITH HATH MADE THEE WHOLE.
teach.b: Then: "Arise, go thy way: thy faith hath made thee whole." All ten were cleansed. Some readers notice that only this one hears he's been made whole.
The healing reached his skin. The thanks reached further.

how: Catholics, Orthodox Christians, Anglicans, Lutherans and others call communion the Eucharist, the thanksgiving; in the United States, some churches read the story of the ten lepers around Thanksgiving.

o: giving thanks: good grace, good gift
a priest's word that the sick are clean
a loud cry asking God for mercy

games.q: what's inside Luke 17:11–19 — tap the pairs.

s: the ten were healed the moment Jesus spoke
"as they went, they were cleansed." they set off while still sick.
the one who came back was a Samaritan
"and he was a Samaritan." Jesus calls him this stranger.
the word Eucharist comes from the Greek for giving thanks
eucharisteo: eu, good, and charis, grace or gift.

games.q: you're one of the ten. halfway to the priests, you look down and your skin is clean. what do you do?
o: keep going to the priests, as you were told.
turn back, praising God loudly, and fall at his feet.
run home to your family first.
games.why: nine kept going. one "turned back, and with a loud voice glorified God," giving thanks. and he was a Samaritan.

practice: Think back over the last year to one good thing you received and walked on from: a recovery, a favor, someone who stood by you when they didn't have to.
Picture yourself turning around on the road, and find the words you'd say to them. If you pray, turn back to God with the same thanks.

wordCard.voice: Eucharisteo, Greek for giving thanks, good grace: what the healed Samaritan did when he turned back, and the root of the word Eucharist.

orig.note: Greek: I give thanks. from eu, good, and charis, grace. the root of Eucharist.

carryVoice: Your line: where are the nine? One came back, and heard he'd been made whole. See you tomorrow.
